messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` verifies that setting a custom Mean implementation in SummaryStatistics works correctly. It creates a SummaryStatistics instance, overrides the mean implementation with a new Mean(), adds values, and asserts the computed mean matches the standalone Mean evaluation. The code for setMeanImpl enforces that the statistics object is empty before setting the new implementation. Then addValue adds values incrementally, including calling meanImpl.increment(value) only if meanImpl is not an instance of Mean (line 158). This design avoids double incrementing when the default Mean is used but would skip updating custom mean implementations of type Mean.

The current bug report notes that calling setVarianceImpl with a Variance overriding implementation causes getStandardDeviation to return NaN. The relevant methods show setVarianceImpl also requires the statistics to be empty, and that getStandardDeviation computes sqrt(getVariance()) if sample size is >1. Since getVariance delegates to the current varianceImpl's getResult(), the issue likely arises if the varianceImpl does not update correctly during addValue calls.

Importantly, addValue only calls varianceImpl.increment(value) if varianceImpl is not an instance of Variance (line 161). If you override variance with a Variance instance, it will skip incrementing it, and thus varianceImpl does not accumulate data, getResult returns NaN or an invalid state, causing getStandardDeviation to also return NaN.

This is essentially the same pattern as the meanImpl logic but reversed: SummaryStatistics was designed with default implementations Mean and Variance but expects custom implementations to be different classes. Overriding with the same class (new Variance()) leads to skipping increments and invalid results.

Hence, the failure to produce a valid standard deviation after overriding varianceImpl with a new Variance arises because addValue does not increment varianceImpl if it is a Variance instance (assuming the default was also Variance). This bug is similar in nature to the non-increment of meanImpl when it's a Mean instance, which the test `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` checks correctly by using a new Mean instance but no addValue increment call is done since that meanImpl is a Mean instance (and mean increment is skipped). The test itself passes because it only checks the getMean, which calls getResult(), but addValue skips meanImpl.increment(value) if it's a Mean instance - the default Mean in the SummaryStatistics class is not of type Mean but some other kind of storeless statistic. But because in setMeanImpl the testing explicitly sets new Mean() implementation, it works because the 'meanImpl' reference is replaced and likely this class handles incrementing.

However, the bug report's problem with varianceImpl stems from skipping increment for varianceImpl instances of Variance class and thus not accumulating the data to compute variance or standard deviation.

To summarize:
- addValue calls varianceImpl.increment only if varianceImpl not instance of Variance.
- Replacing varianceImpl with new Variance() causes increments to be skipped.
- Without increments, getResult returns invalid value (likely NaN), which in turn makes getStandardDeviation return NaN.
- This bug manifests when setVarianceImpl is called with a Variance instance after some data collection, or expected to collect data via addValue.

This analysis fits the bug report and the test code. The existing test checks mean overriding (with no increment due to instance of Mean) without problem, but the variance part has an issue in addValue skipping increments for Variance instances.

The recent bug reports do not relate to this logic and can be ignored.

Recommended place to fix is in SummaryStatistics.addValue ensuring varianceImpl increment is called properly even when varianceImpl is a Variance instance (similarly for meanImpl if necessary), or changing design to avoid this issue. 

This is the root cause of producing NaN standard deviation after setting varianceImpl with a Variance instance.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
